--- title: "Sampling, Standard Error & the Central Limit Theorem" description: "Watch samples become sampling distributions and learn why uncertainty shrinks with sample size." author: "MLStation" date: 2026-10-01 categories: [Statistics, Inference, Simulation] draft: false --- A dataset is one sample. Statistical inference asks: > **What would change if we could repeat the sampling process?** That imaginary repetition creates a **sampling distribution**. ::: {.callout-tip} ## What you will learn - Population, sample, parameter and statistic - Sampling distributions - Standard error - The Central Limit Theorem (CLT) - Why more data reduces uncertainty at a square-root rate ::: ## Three distributions people confuse ```text POPULATION DISTRIBUTION values among individuals SAMPLE DISTRIBUTION values in one observed dataset SAMPLING DISTRIBUTION a statistic across repeated samples ``` For the sample mean, $$ SE(\bar X)=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}. $$ ## Interactive CLT machine The population below is strongly skewed. Increase $n$: the distribution of sample means becomes tighter and more bell-shaped. ```{ojs} //| echo: false viewof nclt = Inputs.range([1,100], {value:5, step:1, label:"Sample size n"}) rclt = d3.randomLcg(.31) means = d3.range(2500).map(()=>{ let s=0; for(let j=0;jd,thresholds:45,fill:"#4F46E5",fillOpacity:.7})),Plot.ruleX([1],{stroke:"#E11D48"})] }) ``` The CLT does **not** say raw data become normal. It says that under suitable conditions, standardized sums/means approach a normal distribution as sample size grows. ## Animation in Python: uncertainty shrinks ::: {#9ef54f8c .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} import numpy as np, pandas as pd import plotly.express as px rng=np.random.default_rng(8) rows=[] for n in [2,5,10,30,100]: means=[rng.exponential(1,n).mean() for _ in range(1200)] rows += [{"n":n,"mean":m} for m in means] df=pd.DataFrame(rows) fig=px.histogram(df,x="mean",animation_frame="n",range_x=[0,3], nbins=45,histnorm="probability density") fig.update_layout(height=380,yaxis_range=[0,4]) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## The square-root law To cut standard error in half: $$ \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n_{\text{new}}}} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} $$ requires $$ n_{\text{new}}=4n. $$ Four times the data for half the standard error. ## DS/ML Bridge Sampling variation appears in: - cross-validation scores, - feature importance estimates, - A/B-test lifts, - offline model metrics, - bootstrap uncertainty, - repeated training/evaluation splits. A model accuracy of 0.91 is a **statistic computed on a sample**, not an eternal property of the model. ## Summary - A statistic changes from sample to sample. - Its sampling distribution quantifies that variability. - Standard error measures uncertainty in an estimator. - The CLT explains why normal approximations are so common. - Uncertainty typically shrinks like $1/\sqrt n$. **Next:** *Estimation, Confidence Intervals & Bootstrap*
